lesson.title: Redemption and Its Costs: The Rise of the Redeemer South
lesson.summary: After federal troops withdrew in 1877, white Democratic Redeemer governments took control of every former Confederate state and systematically dismantled Reconstruction's gains, building the legal and social order that became known as Jim Crow.
lesson.body:
White Southern Democrats who overthrew Reconstruction era Republican governments called themselves Redeemers, framing their return to power as rescuing, or redeeming, the South from what they portrayed as corrupt misrule by Black voters, carpetbaggers, and scalawags. In truth, the Redeemer movement was less a rescue than a calculated campaign to restore white political and economic dominance, and it had already succeeded in several states before the Compromise of 1877 sealed Reconstruction's fate everywhere else. Mississippi Democrats used organized violence and intimidation against Black voters in what became known as the Mississippi Plan of 1875 to retake the state legislature, and in South Carolina, Wade Hampton and his armed Red Shirts followers waged a campaign of violence and voter suppression through the 1876 election that helped force the standoff the Compromise of 1877 eventually resolved.

Redeemer governments relied on the same combination of fraud and violence that groups like the Ku Klux Klan had pioneered during Radical Reconstruction, but once they held full control of state governments, they no longer needed to operate outside the law. They could rewrite it instead.

Over the following two decades, Redeemer legislatures across the South built an elaborate legal architecture to strip Black citizens of the vote without technically violating the Fifteenth Amendment's ban on racial discrimination at the polls. Poll taxes priced out poor voters, literacy tests were administered by white registrars who could fail Black applicants at will while passing illiterate white ones, and grandfather clauses exempted men whose ancestors had voted before Reconstruction, a category that by definition excluded nearly every Black Southerner. Mississippi's 1890 state constitution pioneered many of these techniques, and other Southern states copied its approach over the following decade, effectively nullifying Black political power across the region for two generations.

Alongside disenfranchisement came the system of legal segregation known as Jim Crow, which separated Black and white Southerners in schools, transportation, restaurants, and nearly every other public space, always under the fiction that separate facilities were equal. The Supreme Court gave this system its constitutional blessing in the 1896 case Plessy v. Ferguson, upholding segregation under the doctrine of separate but equal, a ruling that would stand for nearly sixty years.

The Redeemer order produced what came to be called the Solid South, a region of near total one party Democratic control that lasted well into the twentieth century, alongside an expanded convict leasing system that used the Thirteenth Amendment's own punishment exception to funnel disproportionately Black prisoners into forced labor for private companies. This entire structure, built in the years immediately following 1877, remained largely intact until the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s finally forced its dismantling, nearly a century after Redemption began.
